streams.title: Industry size and technology split
streams.narrative:
All figures below are from TRAI's own releases. Latest monthly: August 2026 data (Press Release 125/2026, 28 Sep 2026). Latest quarterly: April–June 2026 performance-indicator report (12 Oct 2026). Yearly 2025-26 report (5 Oct 2026). No September 2026 monthly release existed as of 14 Oct 2026.

Size. Fixed wired broadband (fibre, DSL, cable, Ethernet, leased lines) was 48.63 million (4.86 crore) lines at end-August 2026, up 1.01% in the month. Fixed wireless access (FWA) was 19.34 million (1.93 crore), up 2.68% in the month. Inside FWA, 5G FWA was 13.45 million (Jio 9.42 mn, Airtel 4.03 mn) and Jio's unlicensed-band radio FWA 5.37 million; the rest is small Wi-Fi/radio/satellite ISPs. Mobile broadband was 1,033.24 million. Wired lines are 4.4% of all 1,101.21 million broadband connections, yet carried about 39% of the data TRAI counted in Apr–Jun 2026 (54,303 PB wired vs 84,424 PB mobile).

Growth. Wired broadband at end-March: 22.75 mn (2021), 27.25 (2022), 33.49 (2023), 40.06 (2024), 41.39 (2025), 46.51 (2026). Net adds by financial year: +4.50, +6.24, +6.57, +1.33, +5.12 million. That is 15.4% a year compounded over five years. Caution: the FY2025 number is understated and FY2026 overstated, because TRAI carried Jio's and Airtel's November-2024 filings through to March 2025 when the two did not file. Another 2.12 million wired lines were added in the five months to August 2026.

FWA is the fastest-moving category: 4.89 mn (Mar 2025) to 17.10 mn (Mar 2026, +250%) to 19.34 mn (Aug 2026). Before FY2025 TRAI's "fixed wireless" line held only Wi-Fi/WiMax/radio/VSAT (0.67–1.18 mn), so the series has a break when 5G FWA started. Jio holds about 79% of FWA, Airtel about 21%.

Technology. Fibre is almost all of wired. Of 47.73 mn wired internet lines at June 2026: FTTx 45.14 mn (94.6%), Ethernet/LAN 1.86, leased lines 0.30, DSL 0.25, cable modem 0.18. At March 2025 FTTx was 38.30 of 41.41 mn (92.5%) and DSL 0.62. So the growth is fibre and DSL is disappearing.

Operators (wired broadband, Aug 2026): Jio 14.81 mn (30.5%), Airtel 11.44 (23.5%), BSNL 4.56 (9.4%), ACT 2.48 (5.1%), Kerala Vision 1.56 (3.2%); top five = 71.66%. The June 2026 quarterly table puts "others" at 13.52 mn across hundreds of ISPs; the larger ones are Hathway 1.01 mn, Excitel 0.96, One Broadband (Oneott) 0.92, Netplus 0.84, GTPL 0.76 (+0.20 via KCBPL), Tata Play Broadband 0.65, RailTel 0.61, Alliance 0.57, Asianet 0.46, APSFL 0.39. Five years ago (Mar 2021) BSNL led with 6.82 mn, Airtel had 3.09 and Jio 2.60. Airtel's wired base is 3.7x its March-2021 size; Jio's is 5.7x. Airtel trails Jio by about 3.4 mn wired lines, a gap that has been roughly flat since March 2024 (3.54 mn then, 3.37 mn now).

Circles. TRAI publishes no circle split for wired broadband. The only circle-level fixed-line series is wireline telephones (48.45 mn at Aug 2026). It is not the same thing: Tata Teleservices' 11.2 mn wireline are largely enterprise lines, and BSNL has 6.65 mn wireline but only 4.56 mn wired broadband. With that caveat, Airtel's biggest wireline circles are Delhi 2.57 mn, Karnataka 1.41, Tamil Nadu 1.21, Andhra 1.09; Jio's are Andhra 2.16, Karnataka 1.35, MP 1.23, Delhi 1.19, Mumbai 1.09, Tamil Nadu 1.07. Airtel is ahead of Jio in six circles (Delhi, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Haryana, Punjab); Jio leads the other sixteen. BSNL still leads everyone in Kerala (0.97 mn) and Punjab (0.55 mn).

One trap: total wireline jumped 30% in FY2026 (37.04 to 48.25 mn) mainly because Tata Teleservices' count went from 2.38 to 11.17 mn. That is a reporting change, not new homes connected. Read circle-level wireline growth with that in mind.

gaps: TRAI publishes no circle (LSA) split of wired broadband or FTTH; wireline telephone lines by circle are the only fixed-line circle series, and they differ materially from broadband (Tata Teleservices 11.2 mn mostly enterprise lines; BSNL 6.65 mn wireline vs 4.56 mn wired broadband).

Operator-wise wired broadband is published only for the top five. Figures for Hathway, Excitel, GTPL, Tata Play Broadband, Oneott etc. come from the ISP-wise internet annexure (wired + wireless combined), which TRAI does not label as wired-only.

The technology split (FTTx/DSL/cable/Ethernet/ILL) exists only as chart data labels in the quarterly and yearly reports, not as a table; I read Mar-25, Mar-26 and Jun-26. No technology split by operator or by circle is published.

March 2025 wired figures for Jio and Airtel are their November-2024 filings carried forward (TRAI footnote), so FY2025 net adds (+1.33 mn) are understated and FY2026 (+5.12 mn) overstated; the two years should be read together (+6.45 mn over 24 months).

The FY2026 wireline jump (+30.25%) includes Tata Teleservices' reported base rising from 2.38 to 11.17 mn; TRAI gives no explanation, so circle-level wireline growth in Karnataka and Mumbai should not be read as home-broadband growth.

FWA by operator is published only for 5G FWA (Airtel, Jio) and UBR FWA (Jio); the ~0.5 mn Wi-Fi/radio/satellite ISP fixed-wireless lines have no operator split. The FWA series has a definitional break in FY2025 when 5G FWA entered.
The same August 2026 release gives two FWA totals: 19.34 mn (broadband segment table, includes Wi-Fi/radio/satellite) and 18.82 mn (telephone-connection table, 5G + UBR only).
DoT Annual Report 2025-26 could not be located (searches returned only the 2024-25 report); no DoT figure is used here.
No September 2026 monthly release existed as of 14 Oct 2026; the next TRAI subscription release is expected in late October 2026.
Mar-24 and Mar-25 operator-wise wireline totals were read from image-only annexure pages (they reconcile to the printed All-India totals), not from machine text.
Wired broadband urban/rural split and wired broadband by state are not published; only wireline and total internet have rural/urban tables.
streams.verify_summary:
What I did: the web tool could not read any of the TRAI PDFs directly, so I took the eight copies it downloaded, pulled the text out, and where the numbers sat inside charts I pulled the chart images and looked at them. I opened 8 of the 9 cited documents. I did not get to the March-2021 release (42.pdf).

Safe to quote (seen in the regulator's own documents): figures 1, 2, 3 (end-August 2026 wired 48.63 mn, FWA 19.34 mn with the 5G/UBR and Airtel/Jio split, total 1,101.21 mn); figures 5, 6, 7, 8 (end-March 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025); figure 9 (end-March 2026 wired 46.51 mn, +12.38%); and the three technology splits, figures 12, 13, 14 (FTTx 38.30 -> 43.96 -> 45.14 mn, DSL 0.62 -> 0.25). Figure 11's FWA series is seen at every point except March 2021.

Not safe without a caveat: figure 4 (March 2021) is unchecked, so anything built on it is too - that means in figure 10 the FY22 growth, the five-year +23.76 mn and the 15.4% CAGR are unverified, even though the arithmetic is right. The FY23 to FY26 net additions and the +2.12 mn for April-August 2026 are built only on confirmed numbers and are fine.

Two method traps to state when quoting: (1) TRAI's March-2025 wired figure reuses Jio's and Airtel's November-2024 filings because both missed four months of returns, so FY25's weak +1.33 mn and FY26's strong +5.12 mn are partly a reporting artefact - quote the two years together, not separately. Small wobbles, not errors: the yearly report says wired internet 46.54 mn in its table and 46.55 mn in its text; the FWA series mixes TRAI's telephone-side UBR count (Mar-26 4.29) with its internet-side count (Jun-26 4.99) - the two sides differ by about 0.05 mn each quarter.

streams.title: Airtel Homes
streams.narrative:
Airtel's home broadband business ("Homes") had 14.69 million customers (1.47 crore) at 30 June 2026, the latest reported quarter (Q1 FY27). That is up 33.9% in a year. But net additions in the quarter fell to 473,000, from 1.14 million in the March 2026 quarter and 1.16 million in December 2025. Management says this was deliberate. Cheap entry-priced 5G fixed-wireless (AirFiber) customers churned more, and chip and memory prices made the FWA box "very much more expensive" than fibre. Airtel has pivoted to fibre first and will place FWA only where fibre cannot reach. Regulator data confirms the brake: Airtel added only 83,377 5G FWA users in April to June 2026 against 665,842 the quarter before, and its 5G FWA base was 3.82 million at end-June 2026.

Money. Homes revenue was Rs 22,875 million (Rs 2,288 crore) in Q1 FY27, up 33.2% on a year earlier. FY26 revenue was Rs 77,747 million (Rs 7,775 crore), up 32% on FY25's Rs 59,044 million. The EBITDA margin has stayed between 49% and 50.3% for nine quarters; it was 49.1% in Q1 FY27, the lowest of the nine. ARPU has fallen every quarter, from Rs 572 in June 2024 to Rs 523 in June 2026, because new customers join on cheaper bundled plans. Management says acquisition ARPU is flat and the blended figure is "bottoming out".

Build. Airtel does not print home passes in its quarterly report; the numbers come from earnings calls. 33.5 million (Oct 2024), 35 million (Feb 2025), then "crossed 45 million" at March 2026 after more than 8 million were added in FY26. Quarterly additions rose from 1.5 million (2024) to a stated run-rate of 2.5 million by Nov 2025, with about 2 million in the Dec 2025 quarter. No home-pass figure was given for the June 2026 quarter. Cities covered rose from 1,317 (June 2024) to 1,653 (June 2026). The local cable operator (LCO) model is live in 1,570 cities, and LCO cities are included in that 1,653 total. Airtel does not disclose how many LCO partners it has or the revenue share.

Capex. Homes capex was Rs 43,105 million in FY25 and Rs 68,127 million in FY26 (up 58%), 17% of India capex. Q1 FY27 was Rs 18,996 million, equal to 83% of Homes revenue. Homes EBITDA minus capex has been negative in all nine quarters (minus Rs 7,757 million in Q1 FY27). There is no rupee guidance for homes capex; the stated line is that homes "continues to get its fair share", and in Aug 2026 management spoke of "sharp choices" in homes capex. Unit cost: Gopal Vittal said (Nov 2025) a home pass costs $28 to $32, about 28% to 30% of passes get a customer within a couple of years, so a connected home costs about $100, then comparable with FWA. By May 2026 FWA had become much dearer than that.

Churn is never given as a number. Management says fibre churn is lower, FWA placed in wrong locations churned more, and converged (mobile plus Wi-Fi) customers churn about 50% less. Payback is not disclosed.

Prices (third-party trackers, May to Aug 2026, before 18% GST): fibre Rs 499 (40 Mbps), Rs 799 (100 Mbps data-only), Rs 999 (100 Mbps with Netflix, Prime, Apple TV+), Rs 1,599 (300 Mbps with TV), Rs 3,999 (1 Gbps). AirFiber Rs 699 (40 Mbps), Rs 799 and Rs 899 (100 Mbps), all capped at 1 TB a month. Airtel's own terms page: Rs 1,000 installation on monthly plans, waived on 3, 6 or 12-month plans, with 7.5% and 15% discounts for 6 and 12 months. Airtel's plan pages need a pincode, so prices could not be checked on airtel.in itself.

Outlook statements: a market of 100 million connected homes in four to five years, from about 45 to 46 million now; 95% of the market sits in 400 cities where Airtel has fibre; demand is concentrated in the top 1,000 towns. HSBC (Sep 2026) estimates Homes revenue growing 23% a year over FY26 to FY29 and customers reaching 25.4 million.

Method note: the fetch tool could not read Airtel's PDFs, so the downloaded company files were text-extracted locally. All quarterly numbers are from Airtel's own quarterly reports and call transcripts. The September 2026 quarter (Q2 FY27) is not yet reported as of 14 Oct 2026.

Method: I downloaded the four cited Airtel documents (Q1 FY27 pack, Q4 FY26 pack, Q4 FY25 pack, Q4 FY26 call transcript) and read their text layers page by page; every number below was read off the printed page, not recalled. I used 8 of 8 allowed web calls; one search confirmed no newer quarter exists (Q2 FY27 results are scheduled for 5 Nov 2026), so the Jun-26 quarter is the latest.

Safe to quote (13 of 14 items): every customer, net-add, ARPU, revenue, EBITDA, EBIT, margin, capex, cumulative-investment, cities-covered and LCO-cities figure in items 1-13 matches the investor packs exactly, including the full-year totals, the +19%/+32% revenue growth, the +58% capex growth, the 17% share of India capex and the negative EBITDA-minus-capex figures. Two small derived numbers are arithmetic from printed figures rather than printed themselves (+4.4% QoQ revenue in item 4; the Rs 1 mn rounding gaps in the capex sums in item 11) and both check out. Also safe: the 14 May 2026 statement that Airtel added over 8 million home passes in FY26 to cross 45 million (item 14a), quoted verbatim from the transcript.

Housekeeping, not errors: items 3, 12 and 13 cite only the Q1 FY27 pack, but their older data points (Jun-24 to Mar-25 ARPU and cities; the 1,391 and 1,550 LCO cities) actually sit in the Q4 FY25 and Q4 FY26 packs. Cite those packs for the older points.

Not safe to quote yet: the two older home-pass figures in item 14b (over 33.5 million in Oct 2024; 35 million in Feb 2025). The cited transcript does not contain them, a web search found no source for 33.5 million and found 35 million only as a 2021-22 target, and I ran out of calls before opening the Oct 2024 and Feb 2025 transcripts. The claim that no Jun-26 home-pass figure was given is also unverified because the Q1 FY27 transcript could not be opened. Treat these as 'to be checked', not as wrong.

One category caveat for anyone comparing with regulator data: the Homes customer count is Airtel's own number and mixes fibre and fixed wireless (the pack never splits them and never mentions FWA; the May 2026 call confirms FWA is inside Homes). TRAI publishes Airtel's 5G fixed-wireless subscribers separately, so Airtel's 14.7 million must not be set against TRAI's wired-broadband numbers without saying so.

streams.title: Jio: JioFiber and AirFiber
streams.narrative:
Jio's home broadband is now India's largest, and it is growing mainly through fixed wireless (JioAirFiber), not fibre. At 30 June 2026 (Q1 FY2027) Reliance reported 28.6 million fixed broadband connections (2.86 crore). Of these, 14.0 million (1.40 crore) are AirFiber fixed wireless, about 49%. Jio claims over 43% of India's fixed broadband and over 78% of its fixed wireless. In the 12 months to June 2026 it added 8.6 million homes; 6.6 million of them (77%) came through AirFiber. Source: Reliance's Q1 FY27 release and presentation, 17 July 2026.

Pace. Reliance's own quarter-end series runs 12.4m (Jun-24), 14.1, 15.9, 17.4, 20.0 (Jun-25), ~23, 25+, 27.1, 28.6m (Jun-26). Reported quarterly net adds peaked at about 3 million in Jul–Sep 2025 and 2.5 million in Oct–Dec 2025. Reliance then stopped stating the quarterly figure. Subtracting its own bases gives roughly 1.5–1.8 million in Jan–Mar 2026 and 1.5 million in Apr–Jun 2026. The slowdown is in both products: AirFiber added 1.1 million in Apr–Jun 2026 against 2.1 million in Jul–Sep 2025, and wired JioFiber added only about 0.4 million. These splits are my arithmetic, not Reliance's statements.

Regulator check. TRAI's August 2026 release shows Jio with 14.81 million wired connections (Airtel 11.44m, BSNL 4.56m), 9.42 million 5G fixed wireless (Airtel 4.03m) and 5.37 million unlicensed-band fixed wireless, which only Jio reports. The three add to 29.6 million, consistent with Reliance's 28.6 million two months earlier. Reliance's "fixed broadband" includes fixed wireless; TRAI's "wired" count does not. Share figures from the two are not comparable.

Where. Reliance publishes no homes-passed number and no city count since calling AirFiber "pan-India" in July 2024 (press coverage then said over 5,900 cities). The only geographic split it gives: 70% of new AirFiber connections come from beyond the top 1,000 towns (Oct–Dec 2024). TRAI shows 52% of all 5G fixed wireless connections are rural.

Prices (third-party reading of Jio's tariff sheet, 2 October 2026, before 18% GST): ₹399 for 30 Mbps (fibre only), ₹599 for 30 Mbps with 13 OTT apps and 1,000+ TV channels, ₹899 for 100 Mbps, ₹1,199 for 100 Mbps with Netflix Basic, ₹1,499 for 300 Mbps, ₹3,999 for 1 Gbps. AirFiber slows after 1,000 GB a month; fibre after 3,300 GB. Installation is ₹1,000 on AirFiber, waived with 12 months paid upfront; router and set-top box are included. Jio's own plan pages could not be read, so treat prices as indicative and city-dependent.

Strategy. AGM, 29 August 2025: "Jio will connect every Indian on mobile and home broadband"; AirFiber "adding over one million homes per month". AGM, 19 June 2026: 13 million AirFiber homes; connections "growing at up to 60,000 per day"; over 90% of installs done within 24 hours; new non-line-of-sight equipment; next-generation JioHome at up to 5 Gbps down and 1 Gbps up over AirFiber; a call-back within 15 minutes and Wi-Fi live within 24 hours anywhere in India. The 100-million-homes target appears in the Jan and Apr 2025 decks but was not restated in 2026. Caveat: 60,000 a day is a peak; the Apr–Jun 2026 pace averages about 16,000 a day.

Money. Reliance does not disclose Jio's capex or a home-broadband ARPU. Group capex was ₹1,44,271 crore in FY26 and ₹38,682 crore in Q1 FY27, across all businesses. Blended Jio ARPU was ₹215.6 in Q1 FY27, and management said promotional offers in the homes business held it back. The only AirFiber ARPU figure in public, ₹650–700 a month, is from a January 2025 news report with no named analyst.

Analysts. CLSA (March 2025): 85% of the industry's 2 million home adds in Oct–Dec 2024 were Jio's; Jio was 90% ahead of Airtel. Opensignal (August 2025): Airtel's fixed wireless beat Jio's on every national measure and Jio's "appears to be congested". Jio's own August 2026 release claims 2.5 times the nearest competitor's home adds that month.

Not yet out: Q2 FY27 (Jul–Sep 2026) results, as of 14 October 2026.

findings.metric: Jio Platforms DRHP home broadband disclosures (secondary summary)
findings.value: 27.1m home broadband customers at Mar-26; 42.6% fixed broadband share vs Airtel 22.7%; 67.6% of FY26 industry net adds; FWA 12.9m = 77.5% of 'advanced FWA' market
findings.note: DRHP itself not opened; figures are from IPO-summary sites and agree with the Q4 FY26 release (27.1m, ~13m). Jio Platforms IPO was reported to open 21 Oct 2026.

It does not mention 27.1m, 42.6%, 22.7%, 67.6% or 77.5%, and gives no DRHP filing date (page is 'last updated June 19, 2026'). The 27.1m is independently confirmed by Reliance's Q4 FY26 release, and 42.6%/43% are consistent with Reliance's '~43%'. The Airtel 22.7%, 67.6% and 77.5% figures need the DRHP itself before they are quotable.

streams.verify_summary:
I opened all seven cited Reliance documents (Q1 FY27 release and deck, Q4 FY26 release, and the Jul 2025, Apr 2025, Jan 2026 and Jan 2025 analyst decks) by extracting their text, plus the indmoney DRHP article. The fetch budget is spent; the Oct 2025 and Jul 2024 decks, the Q1 FY27 transcript, the Aug 2026 Jio press release and the DRHP itself were not opened.

SAFE TO QUOTE (seen word-for-word in Reliance documents): 28.6m fixed broadband at Jun-26 with 8.6m added in 12 months; 14.0m AirFiber homes with 6.6m added in 12 months (49%, Reliance says ~50%); 27.1m at Mar-26; the chart series 12.4/14.1/15.9/17.4/20.0 (Jun-24 to Jun-25) and 0.7/1.5/2.9/4.4/5.6/7.4/11.5 (Mar-24 to Dec-25) for AirFiber; quarterly net adds of ~2.0m (Q3 FY25), ~1.5m (Q4 FY25), 2.6m (Q1 FY26), 2.5m (Q3 FY26); market share 41% at Nov-25, ~43% at Mar-26, over 43% at Jun-26; net-add shares of 90% (6 months to Mar-25), ~70% (Q3 FY26), 65%+ (May-25 to May-26, TRAI-based per Reliance's footnote); FWA share ~85% (Mar-25, 5G-based only), ~82% (Jun-25), over 78% (Jun-26); and the Dec-24/Mar-25 restatement warning (~17m and 18m+ later shown as 15.9m and 17.4m).

QUOTE WITH CARE: the AirFiber share of additions. Reliance's own words are 'more than 75%' for both FY26 and the 12 months to Jun-26; 77% (6.6 of 8.6) is a fair computation for the latest 12 months, but '76% of 9.6m' for FY26 is not, because Reliance says FY26 additions were '~10 million', not 9.6m. That same 9.6m error flows into the derived Q4 FY26 range (1.5–1.8m); on Reliance's figures Q4 FY26 is nearer 1.9m and cannot be pinned exactly because Dec-25 is only given as '25 Mn+'. The Q1 FY27 derived additions (1.5m total, ~1.0–1.1m AirFiber) are sound.

NOT YET SAFE: the Sep-25 points (~23m base, 9.5m AirFiber, ~3.0m Q2 FY26 adds, 41% AirFiber share) and the Q1 FY25 figures ('over 1.1m' adds, '>60%' share) were not seen in any opened document. The Aug-26 78.6% FWA share was not checked. Everything attributed to the DRHP via indmoney except '1.29 crore AirFiber connections' is absent from that page, so Airtel's 22.7% share, the 67.6% net-add share, the 77.5% 'advanced FWA' share and the 63.6m-to-150.4m market forecast need the DRHP itself before anyone quotes them.

Two category warnings for anyone writing this up: all 'market share' numbers are Reliance's own claims that mix wired and fixed-wireless broadband, not regulator-published shares; and the FWA share series shifts from '5G-based FWA' (Mar-25) to 'FWA' generally (Jun-25 onward), so the 85%-to-78% decline is not strictly like-for-like.

streams.title: Other operators
streams.narrative:
Outside Jio and Airtel, India's fixed wired broadband market is small and slow-moving. TRAI's August 2026 release puts the total wired base at 48.63 million (4.86 crore). The top five hold 71.66%. The three non-Jio/Airtel names in that top five are BSNL (4.56 million), ACT Fibernet (2.48 million) and Kerala Vision (1.56 million). Everyone else, which means Hathway, GTPL, Tata Play Fiber, Excitel, YOU Broadband, Spectra, DEN, Tata Tele, Vi and thousands of local cable operators, shares about 13.8 million lines. That is my subtraction from TRAI figures, not a TRAI number. This pool grew only about 3.6% between October 2025 and August 2026, while the whole wired market grew 8.5%. Airtel alone grew 15%.

BSNL is the only challenger with national reach. Its wired base rose from 4.42 million (Oct 2025) to 4.56 million (Aug 2026), about +3%. That TRAI figure mixes fibre with old copper DSL. The last fibre-only count I found is 28.67 lakh (2.87 million) from February 2023; nothing newer is published. BSNL sells cheap: the SPARK plan is ₹399 a month for the first year (then ₹449) for 50 Mbps, no OTT. Its growth engine is partners, not staff. Franchisees build and maintain the last mile for a revenue share, and in villages "BharatNet Udyami" entrepreneurs do the same over BharatNet fibre. A third-party page says 2,500+ such partners are onboarded; BSNL has not published that. BharatNet itself is underperforming: 13.23 lakh connections commissioned by March 2026 against an 18 lakh target, only 8.01 lakh in use, and about 7,000 added a month (RTI data via Indian Express). Strength against Airtel: price and rural presence. Weakness: a shrinking landline base (7.46 million in March 2026, down 2.9%), falling revenue (AGR down 3% in FY2026) and service quality.

ACT Fibernet is the strongest regional rival. 2.48 million subscribers in August 2026, up 5.5% since October 2025. It is a southern-cities business: its site lists 35 cities, dominated by Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad and Andhra/Telangana/Tamil Nadu towns, plus Delhi NCR, Jaipur, Lucknow, Pune and Ahmedabad. Expansion is incremental: 19 cities in 2021, about 35 now, mostly smaller southern towns. Entry pricing is about ₹549 for 50 Mbps unlimited (Chennai) and ₹799 for 300 Mbps without OTT. It is private-equity owned; Partners Group took control in 2021 at a USD 1.2 billion valuation. Strength: price per Mbps and brand in Bengaluru and Hyderabad. Weakness: no mobile bundle, no fixed wireless, no presence in most of India.

Kerala Vision is the fifth-largest wired player and the best working model of local cable operators pooling together. 1.56 million subscribers in August 2026, up 9% since October 2025, the fastest growth of the three. It is a co-operative of 6,000 to 7,000 Kerala cable operators, with ₹1,000 crore group revenue (Sep 2025) and about 65% of Kerala's cable TV. Plans start around ₹399 to ₹499. Its broadband is essentially a Kerala business.

The cable MSOs are flat. GTPL Hathway (Gujarat) has 1.07 million broadband subscribers at September 2026, up just 20,000 in a year, on 6 million homes passed. Management has stopped adding homes and is trying to lift conversion from 16-17% to 19-20%. ARPU is ₹470. Hathway Cable (Reliance group) had 1.06 million at March 2025, down from 1.10 million, and its broadband revenue fell 3% to ₹602 crore in FY2025. No June 2026 subscriber count is published. DEN's broadband is marginal (cable modem, 5 to 100 Mbps).

Excitel is the price disruptor. About 1 million users. It turned profitable in FY2026 (₹530 crore revenue, ₹40 crore profit after a ₹70 crore loss). It sells 200 Mbps for ₹466 a month and 300 Mbps with 22 OTT apps and 250+ TV channels for ₹724. But it has pulled back from 55 cities in 2024 to about 7 core cities, exiting Mumbai. Chennai, Pune and Kolkata are planned for early 2027.

Tata Play Fiber (about 20 towns, mostly Mumbai region and Delhi NCR) and YOU Broadband (Vi; 22 Gujarat- and Maharashtra-heavy cities) publish no subscriber numbers. Tata Play prices at a premium: 100 Mbps from ₹700 to ₹800, 1 Gbps at ₹3,600 to ₹4,200 before GST. Spectra's website now presents it as a business-network company.

Net: none of these rivals is adding subscribers at Airtel's pace. The competitive pressure is on price (Excitel, ACT, BSNL) and in specific geographies (Kerala, Gujarat, the southern metros), not on national scale.

streams.title: Households, penetration and outlook
streams.narrative:
THE HOUSEHOLD BASE. India had 24.67 crore (246.7 million) households at Census 2011: 16.79 crore rural, 7.89 crore urban. There has been no official count since. The closest official figure is the weighting behind MoSPI's 2022-23 CAMS survey, which implies 28.36 crore (283.6 million) households: 19.03 crore rural, 9.32 crore urban. MoSPI itself says these survey totals are for ratios, not head-counts. Private 2025 estimates run from 29.6 crore (Helgi Library, citing NSO) to 33.5 crore (dataforindia: 1.4 billion people divided by 4.17 persons per home from HCES 2023-24). Jio's draft prospectus implies about 31.8 crore. Treat 30 to 32 crore as the working range and say it is a range. Urban share of population is about 37 to 38 percent (UN: 37.6 percent in 2026; the official 2011-36 projection reaches 38.6 percent only by 2036).

INTERNET AT HOME. MoSPI's Jan-Mar 2025 telecom survey (CMS:T) found 86.3 percent of households have internet inside the home (rural 83.3 percent, urban 91.6 percent) and 85.5 percent own at least one smartphone. But this is almost entirely mobile. Among connected homes, about 98.8 percent use mobile internet; a fixed line or Wi-Fi connection is present in 24 percent of urban and 9.1 percent of rural connected homes; fibre in 15.3 percent urban and 3.8 percent rural. NFHS-5 (2019-21) found only 33.3 percent of women and 57.1 percent of men aged 15-49 had ever used the internet.

FIXED BROADBAND TODAY. TRAI, end-August 2026: fixed wired 48.63 million; fixed wireless access 19.34 million (of which 5G FWA 13.45 million, 52 percent rural); mobile broadband 1,033 million. These three are separate categories. Wired lines, July 2026: Jio 14.69 million, Airtel 11.28 million, BSNL 4.53 million, ACT 2.47 million. Wireline telephone lines are 89 percent urban, a strong hint that wired broadband is too.

PENETRATION (my arithmetic, inputs stated). Wired 48.63 million divided by 283.6 million homes = 17.1 percent of households; wired plus FWA 67.97 million = 24.0 percent. On a 335 million denominator the same numbers are 14.5 and 20.3 percent. Jio's DRHP puts fixed broadband (including FWA) at about 20 percent of households at March 2026, urban about 42 percent, rural about 6 percent, against more than 70 percent globally excluding India. On the ITU per-100-people measure (2024): India 3.15, Indonesia 4.92, Vietnam 23.71, Brazil 24.08, China 47.19; world 20 per 100 (2025).

OUTLOOK. I found no published industry-level FY2027 fixed broadband forecast from ICRA, CRISIL (current), CareEdge, Omdia, Analysys Mason, Ookla, Jefferies, Kotak, Nomura or Motilal Oswal. What is published: HSBC (reported Feb 2026): home broadband 40 million in FY24 to 114 million by FY30, about 19 percent a year. Jio DRHP (Oct 2026): 63.6 million FY26 to 150.4 million FY31, 18.8 percent a year, household penetration to about 46 percent. Orient Cables RHP (Sept 2026): 46.5 million FY26 to 110-126 million FY31. GlobalData (Nov 2025, Apr 2026): FWA 21.4 million by 2030 at 21.4 percent a year; FWA share of fixed broadband 15.3 percent in 2025 to 27.5 percent in 2030; fibre about 63 percent of lines in 2030. JM Financial (Feb 2026), Airtel only: 14.4 million FY26E, 18.6 million FY27E, 22.8 million FY28E. Airtel management: connected homes to double to 100 million from 40-50 million (59 million at Nov 2025). One caution: CRISIL's Jan 2024 call of about 39 million wired lines by FY26 undershot; the actual end-FY26 wired base was about 46.5 to 47 million. The mix is also shifting: Airtel's 5G FWA additions fell from 665,842 (Jan-Mar 2026) to 83,377 (Apr-Jun 2026) as it pivoted to fibre, while Jio added 530,247 and its AirFiber passed 14 million.

DEMAND DRIVERS. 601 million OTT viewers and 148.2 million active paid OTT subscriptions (subscriptions, not homes; Ormax, Sept 2025). 68 million connected-TV households, 40 million active weekly, up from 30 million (FICCI-EY, Mar 2026); Ormax estimates 35-40 million CTV homes. 515-525 million online gamers in 2025. Work from home: 14 percent of Indian workers fully remote, 36 percent hybrid (ADP 2025), but 52 percent of firms are now fully office-based (CBRE 2025). No published multi-device household figure was found.

AFFORDABILITY. Per-capita NSDP 2024-25 (current prices): Sikkim Rs 7.64 lakh, Goa 7.09 lakh, Delhi 5.53 lakh, Chandigarh 4.94 lakh, Telangana 4.28 lakh, Karnataka 4.22 lakh, Tamil Nadu 4.04 lakh, Haryana 3.94 lakh, Gujarat 3.71 lakh, Maharashtra 3.54 lakh, Kerala 3.46 lakh, Himachal 3.08 lakh, Puducherry 3.06 lakh, Andhra Pradesh 2.98 lakh, Uttarakhand 2.96 lakh. All-India Rs 2.35 lakh. Bottom: Bihar Rs 0.76 lakh, Uttar Pradesh 1.24 lakh. These come from a secondary table citing PRS/RBI and were not cross-checked against the RBI Handbook.

streams.title: Where each operator is strong
streams.narrative:
WHAT EXISTS BELOW NATIONAL LEVEL. The only official sub-national fixed-line table is TRAI's wireline count by licensed circle (22 circles) and operator. It sits in the monthly subscription release (Annexure-I) and the quarterly report. Newest: end-August 2026, released 28 Sep 2026. Three cautions. (1) It counts fixed telephone lines, so it includes Tata Teleservices' 11.2 million lines, mostly business lines. (2) It excludes 5G/AirFiber-type connections, which TRAI counts as wireless FWA, in a separate circle table. (3) It leaves out ISP-only players (ACT, Hathway, Excitel, Kerala Vision, GTPL), whose fixed broadband is published only nationally. So it maps the Airtel-vs-Jio-vs-BSNL home-fibre race, not all fixed broadband. Every row below was checked against TRAI's printed totals.

WHERE AIRTEL IS STRONG (fixed lines, Aug 2026). Airtel leads only 2 of 22 circles: Delhi (2.57 million lines, 48.8%) and Tamil Nadu (1.21 million, 31.3%). It is a clear second in Bihar (31.1%), UP East (30.3%), Rajasthan (29.7%), MP (28.8%), Maharashtra ex-Mumbai (28.2%), Haryana (27.6%) and Punjab (25.1%). Weakest: Kerala 10.1%, Mumbai 12.8%, Gujarat 14.5%, Kolkata 15.1%, Odisha 15.5%, West Bengal 17.0%. Jio leads 13 circles and has over half the lines in UP West (59.9%), West Bengal (56.0%), UP East (55.3%), Bihar (52.9%), MP (51.0%), plus Assam, J&K and North East. BSNL still leads Kerala (58.5%), Haryana, Himachal and Punjab. Tata's business lines make it the nominal leader in Mumbai (50.5%), Karnataka (45.3%) and Maharashtra (35.9%).

5G FIXED WIRELESS BY CIRCLE (Aug 2026; only Airtel and Jio report). Airtel holds more than half of 5G FWA lines in just two circles: Mumbai (53.3%) and Tamil Nadu (51.5%). Near parity in Delhi (46.3%) and Karnataka (41.8%). Jio has 75-85% in West Bengal, Bihar, Himachal, Odisha, MP, UP East, UP West and J&K. Nationally: Airtel 4.03 million 5G FWA (30%), Jio 9.42 million, plus 5.37 million Jio-only unlicensed-band FWA. Airtel said in Aug 2026 it will put fibre first in the roughly 400 cities holding about 95% of demand and use FWA only where fibre cannot reach; its 5G FWA additions fell to 83,377 in Apr-Jun 2026 from 665,842 the quarter before.

MOMENTUM. In August 2026 alone Airtel out-added Jio in fixed lines in Delhi (+17,331 vs +5,099), Maharashtra (+20,489 vs +12,133), Tamil Nadu (+11,146 vs +4,028), Punjab and Haryana. Jio out-added Airtel in Karnataka (+45,312 vs +12,427), MP (+29,709 vs +9,469) and AP (+25,211 vs +8,870). Airtel lost 4,485 lines in Mumbai. Over FY2026, Karnataka's wireline base grew 67% to 6.14 million, Mumbai 51%, Maharashtra 48%, Gujarat 41% (TelecomLead on TRAI data); Tata's business lines are a large part of Karnataka and Mumbai, so this is not all home fibre.

REGIONAL ISPs (TRAI national counts, but each is a one-region player). Kerala Vision 1.56 million (Aug 2026) is bigger than BSNL's 0.97 million Kerala lines, so Kerala's fixed broadband is really led by local ISPs (Asianet adds 0.46 million). GTPL 0.76m + 0.19m (Gujarat, West Bengal), Netplus 0.82m (Punjab), Alliance 0.56m (Kolkata/WB), APSFL 0.41m (AP). ACT has 2.48 million customers and lists 35 cities; Hathway 1.02 million, 11 cities; Excitel 0.96 million, 60+ mostly UP/Telangana/Haryana towns and "close to one million households in 50+ cities"; Tata Play Fiber 0.63 million, 18 cities. None publishes a city split; city lists are presence only.

CITY-LEVEL EVIDENCE is thin. Ookla (Feb 2025): median fixed download Delhi 91 Mbps, Mumbai 58 Mbps. Opensignal (Feb-May 2025, by circle): Excitel fastest fixed line in Delhi, AP and Karnataka; GTPL in Gujarat; Asianet in Kerala; ACT in Tamil Nadu; Airtel in Mumbai; Airtel won every FWA award in all 20 circles. Odisha is the one state with an operator split: Jio 3.79 lakh (379,000) JioFiber plus 4.16 lakh (416,000) AirFiber at June 2026, about 80% of the state's FWA, consistent with TRAI's circle table.

EXPANSION SIGNALS 2025-26. Jio: 28.6 million fixed broadband, 14.0 million AirFiber homes (June 2026), non-line-of-sight hardware to widen reach. Airtel: 14.7 million Homes customers (June 2026), fibre pivot. Excitel: new CEO March 2026, cable-operator partnerships and new markets. GTPL: entered Kerala and J&K (TV) and is buying ACT Group's cable-TV units (not broadband). No official Jio AirFiber town count was found; the "7,000+ towns" in Reliance's deck is its retail stores.

Bottom line: all 14 figures are safe to quote. Every number, share and date in the research stream matches TRAI Press Release No. 125/2026 (dated 28 September 2026, "Highlights of Telecom Subscription Data at the end of August 2026"), and this is the newest release — the end-September data is not out yet (TRAI has been publishing on the 28th of the following month, so expect it around 28 October 2026).

1. Delhi "incl. NCR towns": TRAI's footnote says the Ghaziabad/Noida/Gurgaon/Faridabad inclusion applies to WIRELESS data; it does not say so for wireline. The Delhi wireline numbers are right; the bracket is unsupported — drop it or say 'Delhi service area'.

Nothing was refuted or needed correcting.

streams.title: Unit economics of a home pass
streams.narrative:
What the model can stand on, and what it cannot

Home passes and take-up (fixed wired FTTH). Airtel said on its Q4 FY26 call (May 2026) that it rolled out "upwards of 8 million home passes" in FY26 to cross 45 million passes. Its Homes customer base was 14.22 million at March 2026 and 14.69 million at June 2026, but that base counts both fibre (FTTH) and 5G fixed wireless (FWA) customers. Airtel's FWA base was about 3.74 million at March 2026. Subtracting it, Airtel had roughly 10.5 million fibre customers on 45 million-plus passes: about 23 customers per 100 passes. That ratio is my arithmetic from Airtel's numbers, not an Airtel disclosure. Management's only stated take-up assumption is from August 2022: about 30% utilisation of a pass over 18 to 24 months. Jio does not publish a home-pass count, so no customer-per-pass figure can be computed for Jio. Jio had 28.6 million fixed broadband customers at June 2026, of which over 14 million were AirFiber (FWA); FWA produced over 75% of its additions in the past year.

Cost per home passed. No operator or analyst publishes a current rupee figure. The best dated anchors are: Airtel CEO Gopal Vittal in May 2023, "cost per connected home pass" of $100 to $120 (roughly Rs 8,000 to 10,000 at that time; my conversion), lower on the local-cable-operator (LCO) side; and an August 2022 Business Standard piece quoting unnamed sources at Rs 12,000 per pass, doubling to Rs 24,000 per connected home at 50% take-up. An older E&Y figure of $1,580 (Rs 1.1 lakh) per household is undated and should not be used for 2026. Nobody splits dense urban buildings from plotted areas in rupees; management only says cities are cheaper and "difficult terrains" much costlier.

A rupee cross-check from Airtel's own segment table: Homes capex was Rs 6,813 crore in FY26 against about 8 million passes added and 4.18 million customers added. That is at most about Rs 8,500 per pass added, but the figure also contains routers, drop cables and LCO equipment, so it is an upper bound, not a pass cost.

Connect cost. The customer-side charges are published: Airtel charges Rs 1,000 installation on monthly plans, waived on 3, 6 and 12-month plans; the router stays Airtel's property; monthly-billed fibre customers pay a Rs 1,500 advance adjusted against bills. Jio AirFiber waives its Rs 1,000 installation for annual plans and gives the CPE free. The operator's own cost of the fibre ONT and drop is not disclosed by anyone. For FWA, the CPE has been quoted at $200 (2022), $170 to 180 (2023) and $130 to 150 (2024). Airtel said in December 2024 that FWA and FTTH unit economics had become "comparable", then in May and August 2026 said memory and chipset prices made FWA "very much more expensive", and pivoted to fibre first, with "almost 95%" of the market in 400 cities.

ARPU and margins. Airtel Homes ARPU was Rs 523 in Q1 FY27, down each quarter from Rs 543 in Q4 FY25. Homes EBITDA margin has sat near 50% (FY25 49.9%, FY26 50.1%, Q1 FY27 49.1%). EBIT margin fell from 17.2% to 11.0% year on year as depreciation grew. Homes capex exceeded Homes EBITDA in every one of the last five quarters; FY26 operating free cash flow was minus Rs 2,918 crore. Jio does not report a fixed broadband ARPU or margin; its blended ARPU was Rs 215.6 and it said fixed-broadband promotions diluted it.

streams.verify_summary:
Verdict in one line: 11 of 14 figures check out word-for-word against the cited Airtel documents and articles; one (the FWA count) needs its sourcing fixed; two derived numbers are sound arithmetic, but one of them leans on that FWA count.

Method note: the three Airtel PDFs (Q4 FY26 transcript, Q4 FY26 investor pack, Q1 FY27 investor pack) came back from the fetch tool as raw binary, so I extracted their text locally from the downloaded copies (text saved under the session scratchpad, txt/ folder) and read the Homes tables and the home-pass passage directly. critic.summary:
What is solid: the national picture. TRAI's August 2026 size and operator shares, the fibre-vs-FWA split, Airtel's Homes P&L, and the circle-level 5G FWA table all checked out against the regulator's and company's own documents. Sections 1, the national half of 2, and the revenue/margin half of 8 can be written with confidence.

The three biggest holes:

1. Nothing below circle level, and the brief is about cities and localities. No public source gives any Indian city's broadband subscribers by operator. The one state table is telephone lines: it counts Tata's 11 million business lines, leaves out ACT, Kerala Vision, Excitel and every fixed-wireless connection, and has nothing for Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune or Gurugram. Sections 2 (city and micro-market), 5 and 7 cannot be built from public data. They need Airtel's own pass and connect data by city and locality, especially connects per 100 existing passes, or they must be labelled modelled and shown with sensitivity.

2. The money numbers are missing or stale. The digest's own cost-per-pass anchors disagree by three to five times (about Rs 2,500, Rs 8,500 and Rs 12,000) and none is current or splits apartment blocks from plotted colonies; the take-up rate is a 2022 remark; churn, acquisition cost, payback and return on capital are published by nobody. Section 8 will be 100% assumptions. That is fine only if every assumption is named as one and the capex range (roughly Rs 13 to 60 crore for 5 lakh passes) is shown rather than a single confident figure.

3. The forward view has no anchor. No research house publishes an FY2027 industry forecast; the household base is a 28-to-34 crore range that moves penetration by 3-4 points; Jio's plans, the fixed-wireless cost shock and the ARPU path are unquantified; and three releases (TRAI September data around 28 Oct, Reliance's September quarter within weeks, Airtel's on 5 Nov) will overtake the report within three weeks of its date. Section 3 needs explicitly modelled low/base/high cases and an 'as of' stamp with a refresh step.

Two framing points the report must state. First, 5 lakh passes is about 6% of the 8 million-plus Airtel laid last year, roughly three weeks of its build pace, so the question is where, not whether, and 'where' is exactly where the evidence is thinnest; the brief owner should also say whether the 5 lakh is extra money or a reallocation. Second, six different definitions of 'home broadband' are in circulation (TRAI wired, TRAI wired plus FWA, telephone lines, Reliance fixed broadband including FWA, Airtel Homes including FWA, analyst home broadband). Without one reconciliation table, the report will contain share and growth sentences that are false even when the arithmetic is right.
